def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    # Knife-edge decider-direction contrast at balanced tally margins.
    #
    # For every trial we compute (a) the tally margin m = (#features A wins)
    # - (#features B wins), and (b) the winner implied by the advocated
    # misbinding-TTB cascade (subjective hierarchy = instructed validities
    # reversed end-to-end: cue order f4 -> f0 -> f2 -> f1 -> f3 -> f5).
    #
    # We keep only trials with |m| in {0, 3} (excluding the |m|=1 cells,
    # whose decider directions are unbalanced across margins) and where the
    # cascade has a discriminating cue. In this subset the misbinding-A
    # cells are {T1 (m=-3), T3 (m=0), T5 (m=+3), T9 (m=0), T10 (m=0)} and
    # the misbinding-B cells are {T6 (m=+3), T7 (m=0), T8 (m=-3), T11 (m=0),
    # T12 (m=0)} -- perfectly mirror-balanced in margin.
    #
    # Metric = P(choose A | cascade says A) - P(choose A | cascade says B).
    #
    # Under Tallying, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*m) + eps/2, which is
    # exactly symmetric in m. Within each group the margins are balanced
    # (-3/+3 pairs and 0s), so BOTH group means are exactly 0.5 for ANY
    # (beta, epsilon) -- the metric is pinned to 0 parameter-free.
    #
    # Under misbinding TTB, p(A) = p_follow on cascade-A cells and
    # 1 - p_follow on cascade-B cells, so the metric equals 2*p_follow - 1,
    # which over the advocated parameter ranges lies in ~[0.27, 0.44]
    # (mean ~0.36) regardless of margin.

    df = data.reset_index(drop=True)
    a_lists = df['option_a_ratings'].tolist()
    b_lists = df['option_b_ratings'].tolist()
    resp = df['response'].to_numpy()

    # Design validities and the kappa=1 reversed subjective hierarchy.
    val = np.array([0.6, 0.95, 0.6, 0.85, 0.65, 0.9])
    w = val[::-1]
    cue_order = np.argsort(-w, kind='stable').tolist()  # -> [4, 0, 2, 1, 3, 5]

    a_side = []  # trials where the misbound cascade favors A
    b_side = []  # trials where the misbound cascade favors B

    for i in range(len(df)):
        av = [int(v) for v in a_lists[i]]
        bv = [int(v) for v in b_lists[i]]
        n = len(av)

        margin = (sum(1 for j in range(n) if av[j] > bv[j])
                  - sum(1 for j in range(n) if bv[j] > av[j]))
        if abs(margin) == 1:
            # Unbalanced decider directions at |m|=1; excluded so the
            # Tallying expectation stays exactly 0.
            continue

        winner = -1
        for j in cue_order:
            if j >= n:
                continue
            if av[j] > bv[j]:
                winner = 0
                break
            if bv[j] > av[j]:
                winner = 1
                break
        if winner == -1:
            continue  # full-tie trial (T16): no discriminating cue

        chose_a = 1.0 if resp[i] == 0 else 0.0
        if winner == 0:
            a_side.append(chose_a)
        else:
            b_side.append(chose_a)

    pa = float(np.mean(a_side)) if len(a_side) > 0 else 0.5
    pb = float(np.mean(b_side)) if len(b_side) > 0 else 0.5
    return float(pa - pb)
metric.rationale: The metric exploits a parameter-free knife-edge of Tallying: its choice probability depends only on the tally margin m via a symmetric sigmoid, p(A|-m) = 1 - p(A|m). I select the 10 trial cells whose tally margins are balanced across the misbinding cascade's decider direction: cascade-A cells {T1 (m=-3), T3, T9, T10 (m=0), T5 (m=+3)} and cascade-B cells {T8 (m=-3), T7, T11, T12 (m=0), T6 (m=+3)}. Within each group the margins are exactly mirrored, so under Tallying both P(choose A) group means equal 0.5 for ANY (beta, epsilon) in its ranges — the metric is identically 0 in expectation, with only binomial sampling noise (sd ~0.13 per subject over 30 trials per side). Under the advocated misbinding TTB, every one of these cells is decided by the first cue of the reversed hierarchy, so P(choose A | cascade-A) = p_follow and P(choose A | cascade-B) = 1 - p_follow, giving metric = 2*p_follow - 1, which lies in ~[0.27, 0.44] across the advocated beta/epsilon ranges (mean ~0.36) and is flat in margin. The between-theory mean gap (~0.36) is large relative to per-subject noise (~0.12-0.13 sd), so with N=25 subjects Welch's t is expected around 8-11, far below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on a single subject's slice (each subject completes all 16 cells x 6 reps, so both groups are always populated), giving a well-defined between-subject variance. Unlike an overall agreement rate (which extreme-beta Tallying could push toward 0.6, eroding the gap) or a single-cell contrast (noisy), this contrast cannot be attenuated by any Tallying parameterization because Tallying's prediction is exactly 0 by symmetry.

Tallying ignores validities entirely: p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*m) + eps/2, depending only on margin m. Misbinding TTB emits a constant follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which over its parameter ranges (beta in [0.6,1.2], eps in [0.08,0.18]) lies in [0.62, 0.75] toward the first discriminating cue in the order f0,f5,f3,f1,f2,f6,f4. SIGNATURE 1 - THE ORTHOGONAL FACTORIAL GRID (T1-T10): the misbound TOP cue f0 (advertised only 60%) always decides, toward A in T1-T5 and toward B in T6-T10 (exact A/B mirrors), while the margin sweeps -3, -1, 0, +1, +3. This is a fully balanced 2 (decider direction) x 5 (margin) design, and the two theories predict TRANSPOSED main-effect structures in the marginal means: Tallying predicts a NULL decider-row effect (both row means exactly 0.5, since margins are symmetric within each row) with a strictly graded margin-column effect passing through EXACTLY 0.5 at m=0; misbinding TTB predicts a strong decider-row effect (~0.70 vs ~0.30) with a NULL margin-column effect (every column mean exactly 0.5). SIGNATURE 2 - SINGLE-CELL DISJOINT PREDICTION INTERVALS AT EXTREME MARGINS (T14, T15): on T14, ALL six other experts - including the 95% expert - favor A (margin +5) and only the first-listed 60% expert favors B. T15 is the exact mirror (margin -5, lone 60% expert favors A): Tallying <= 0.44, misbinding >= 0.62. These cells also separate misbinding from STANDARD TTB (which follows the 95% expert to A on T14), making the design adversarial to the whole TTB family. SIGNATURE 3 - PARAMETER-FREE KNIFE EDGES WITH COMPOSITION CONTROL (T3, T8, T11): three margin-0 cells - a 2-2 tally with decider f0->A (T3), its mirror with decider f0->B (T8), and a sparse 1-1 tally with decider f0->A (T11). Tallying is pinned to EXACTLY 0.50 on all three regardless of (beta, eps) and regardless of tally composition; misbinding predicts ~0.70/~0.30 splits on all three, invariant to whether 2 or 6 cues sit on each side. SIGNATURE 4 - DECIDER-VALIDITY AND DEPTH INVARIANCE AT FIXED MARGIN (T2, T12, T13): three margin-+1 cells whose misbound deciders are the 60% first-listed expert at depth 1 (T2), the 90% expert at depth 4 (T12), and the 95% expert at depth 6 (T13, where it is the ONLY discriminating cue). Misbinding predicts the SAME follow rate on all three - the follow probability cannot depend on the decider's advertised accuracy or cascade depth; any monotone validity gradient (e.g., following the lone 95% expert more than the 60% expert) falsifies the kappa=1 misbinding claim. Tallying also predicts identical values here (same margin), so these cells isolate the competitor's internal structure. GLOBAL PROFILES: misbinding TTB emits a two-level step function over the 16 cells (~[0.62,0.75] toward the misbound decider on all 15 discriminating trials, exactly 0.5 on the full tie), invariant to margin, tally composition, cascade depth, and decider validity; Tallying emits a monotone psychometric function of margin with exact 0.5 on the three margin-0 cells, exact equality within margin levels (T1=T10-margin... specifically T1=T10? No: T1 (m=+3, dec->A) = T10 (m=+3, dec->B) in p(A); T2=T9=T12=T13; T5=T6; T14 highest, T15 lowest), and values far outside the misbinding cap on T14/T15. The profiles are structurally disjoint - e.g., misbinding says p(T15)=p(T1) (both decider->A) while Tallying says p(T15) <= 0.44 < 0.56 <= p(T1); misbinding says p(T3)=p(T2) while Tallying says p(T3)=0.5 < p(T2) - so model comparison on the full 16-cell response profile separates the theories even after fitting beta and epsilon to each. T16 (full tie) anchors lapse rate and side bias (both theories: exactly 0.5). With 16 unique pairs and K = 6 (96 trials exactly), each cell yields 6 repetitions per subject for stable per-subject choice proportions.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Design-time constants for this experiment.
VALIDITIES = np.array([0.6, 0.9, 0.8, 0.95, 0.65, 0.75, 0.6])


def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    """Cue-following deviation from chance on tally-tied (margin-0) trials.

    For every trial whose tally margin is zero (A and B win on equal numbers
    of features), find the first strictly discriminating cue under the
    reversed-hierarchy cue order (the competing theory's subjective
    hierarchy). Record whether the subject's choice followed that cue.
    Tallying predicts exactly chance (0 deviation) on every tied trial,
    for ANY (beta, epsilon). One-reason misbinding predicts a systematic
    follow rate of p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, i.e. a deviation of
    roughly +0.12 to +0.25 above chance.
    """
    # Reversed-hierarchy subjective weights and cue order (stable ties).
    w = VALIDITIES[::-1].astype(float)
    cue_order = np.argsort(-w, kind="stable")

    a_col = data["option_a_ratings"].tolist()
    b_col = data["option_b_ratings"].tolist()
    resp_col = data["response"].tolist()

    follows = []
    for a_raw, b_raw, r_raw in zip(a_col, b_col, resp_col):
        a = np.asarray(a_raw, dtype=float)
        b = np.asarray(b_raw, dtype=float)
        if a.shape != b.shape or a.ndim != 1:
            continue

        # Tally margin: number of features A wins minus number B wins.
        margin = int(np.sum(a > b) - np.sum(b > a))
        if margin != 0:
            # Only tied tallies carry the parameter-free signature.
            continue

        # First discriminating cue under the reversed hierarchy.
        decider = None
        for j in cue_order:
            if a[j] > b[j]:
                decider = 0  # cue favors A
                break
            if b[j] > a[j]:
                decider = 1  # cue favors B
                break
        if decider is None:
            # Full tie (T16): both theories say 0.5; no information.
            continue

        resp = int(r_raw)
        follows.append(1.0 if resp == decider else 0.0)

    if len(follows) == 0:
        return 0.0

    # Deviation of the tied-trial cue-follow rate from chance.
    return float(np.mean(follows)) - 0.5
metric.rationale: The design contains exactly four tally-tied (margin-0) cells: T3, T8, T11, and the full tie T16. Tallying's softmax over equal counts is EXACTLY uniform for any (beta, epsilon), so its probability of choosing in the direction of any particular cue on a tied trial is exactly 0.5 — a parameter-free knife-edge. The reversed-hierarchy one-reason model instead always follows the first discriminating cue in its misbound order (f3, f5, f4, f1, f2, f0, f6): on T3 and T11 the decider points to B, on T8 to A, so its tied-trial follow rate is the cascade-follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, which lies in [0.62, 0.75] over its parameter ranges. The metric pools all tied trials that possess a discriminating cue (3 cells x 6 reps = 18 trials per subject), codes each choice as 'followed the misbound decider' or not, and returns the follow rate minus 0.5. Expected values: Tallying ~ 0.00 (per-subject variance only binomial, ~0.25/18 = 0.014); misbinding ~ +0.18 (variance ~0.013). With N=25 the Welch t-statistic is ~5.5 (p ~ 1e-6) at typical misbinding parameters, and still ~3.6 (p < 0.001) at its worst-case corner (beta=0.6, eps=0.18), safely below alpha=0.01. The metric avoids all parameter-dependent contrasts (e.g., psychometric slope over margins), because Tallying's beta range [0.1, 20] is wide and a slope-based metric could flip sign or collapse; the tied-trial contrast is the unique signature that is exactly zero under Tallying for every parameter setting, while strictly positive under one-reason deciding. It works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's 96-trial slice, so the between-subject variance is well defined.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by counting, across all features, how often one option has a higher value than the other. The option that wins on more features is chosen. Tallying discards cardinal magnitudes — only the sign of each feature-wise comparison matters — so the heuristic is robust to monotone rescaling of individual features and cannot be swayed by a single large feature difference in the way Equal-Weight can. Ties on an individual feature contribute nothing to either count: that cue is simply treated as uninformative for the pair. No feature is privileged, in contrast to Take The Best; every cue contributes equally to the tally. When the two counts are equal the heuristic has no basis for preference and the learner must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the two tallies with inverse temperature beta (interpolating between fully deterministic choice at large beta and uniform guessing at beta = 0), plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Tallying heuristic (Dawes 1979; Gigerenzer &
    # Goldstein 1999). Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors
    # for the current trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features),
    # with row 0 = option A, row 1 = option B. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Tallying expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    # Count strict feature-wise wins; ties contribute to neither option.
    a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
    b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
    scores = np.array([a_wins, b_wins])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. When
    # a_wins == b_wins the softmax is exactly uniform regardless of
    # beta, which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating
    # tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

next_theory.description: Weakest-Expert-First Frugality (value-based anti-validity TTB). People are one-reason decision makers: they consult cues one at a time and let the first strictly discriminating cue decide, ignoring all lower cues and all magnitude/tally information. However, the subjective cue hierarchy is anti-correlated in VALUE with the instructed validities: subjects systematically consult the cue with the LOWEST advertised validity first, then the next-lowest, and so on (equivalently, subjective weights w_j = -validity_j). Because no integration across cues occurs, the model predicts a flat choice profile across tally margins (zero psychometric slope). When no cue discriminates, the model guesses uniformly. Validity ties are broken by a free per-subject tie-breaking parameter (early-position vs late-position preference among equally weak cues). Response noise enters through a softmax with inverse temperature beta over the binary winner score, plus an independent lapse epsilon mixing in a uniform choice, giving an implied cascade-follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 that spans roughly 0.54 to 0.86 across subjects with a mean near 0.70 — high enough to produce the steep contrasts in the non-monotone-validity experiments while moderate values cover the monotone ones.
next_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, state, history):
    # Weakest-Expert-First Frugality (value-based anti-validity TTB).
    # One-reason decision making: cues are consulted one at a time and
    # the first strictly discriminating cue decides. The subjective
    # hierarchy is anti-correlated in VALUE with the instructed
    # validities: the cue with the LOWEST advertised validity is
    # consulted FIRST, then the next-lowest, etc. (subjective weights
    # w_j = -validity_j). This is a VALUE-based sort (ascending
    # validity), not a positional reversal of the validity list, so in
    # experiments where the validity list is not monotone in feature
    # position the two hierarchies genuinely differ. No integration
    # across cues occurs -> flat psychometric profile across tally
    # margins. Noise: softmax (inverse temperature beta) over the
    # binary winner score, plus an independent lapse epsilon mixing in
    # a uniform choice. History is ignored (no feedback in this task).
    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )
    n_features = stim.shape[1]

    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])
    tie_break = float(parameters["tie_break"])

    # Weakest-expert-first hierarchy: sort cues by ASCENDING validity
    # value. Ties in validity are broken by the free tie_break
    # parameter: 0 -> earlier feature position first (stable),
    # 1 -> later feature position first among equally weak cues.
    # np.lexsort uses the LAST key as primary: primary = val ascending,
    # secondary = position (forward or reversed).
    pos = np.arange(n_features)
    secondary = pos if tie_break < 0.5 else (n_features - 1 - pos)
    cue_order = np.lexsort((secondary, val))

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    winner = None
    for j in cue_order:
        if a[j] > b[j]:
            winner = 0
            break
        if b[j] > a[j]:
            winner = 1
            break

    n_opts = 2
    if winner is None:
        # No discriminating cue — pure guess (lapse mixing leaves a
        # uniform unchanged).
        return np.ones(n_opts) / float(n_opts)

    scores = np.array([1.0, 0.0]) if winner == 0 else np.array([0.0, 1.0])

    # Numerically stable softmax over the binary winner score: the
    # winner's probability is sigmoid(beta). The implied cascade-follow
    # probability is p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, which over the
    # sampled (beta, epsilon) ranges spans ~[0.54, 0.86] across
    # subjects with a mean near 0.70.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / float(n_opts))
next_theory.rationale: The arbiter diagnosed the fatal flaw of the pi_3 family: it implemented the anti-validity hierarchy by POSITIONALLY reversing the communicated validity list. In the six monotone-validity experiments (where validity decreases with feature index) positional reversal coincides with ascending-validity sorting, so pi_3_2 succeeded there; but in the two non-monotone experiments (presented Experiments 7 and 8) positional reversal wrongly promotes mid- and high-validity cues to the top of the hierarchy (f4 at 0.65 in Experiment 7; f3 at 0.95 in Experiment 8), producing strongly POSITIVE metric values where the real data are strongly NEGATIVE (-0.31 and -0.29). The fix is to compute the anti-correlation on validity VALUES: sort cues by ascending true validity. I verified analytically that this flips both signatures: in Experiment 7 the metric becomes (7-14q)/12 (e.g., -0.245 at q=0.70, vs real -0.311, where pi_3_2 predicted +0.36); in Experiment 8 the single margin-0 cell T11 has the weakest cue f0 favoring A while the positional-reversal decider is f5 favoring B, so the metric becomes 0.5-q (e.g., -0.20 at q=0.70, vs real -0.289, where pi_3_2 predicted +0.19). Meanwhile, in every monotone-validity experiment the ascending-value order is IDENTICAL to the positional reversal, so the already-good predictions of pi_3_2 on Experiments 1-6 are preserved exactly (Experiment 1 metric = 1-q; Experiment 3 = 2q-1; Experiment 4 = 4q-2; Experiment 5 = q; Experiment 6 = 2q-1). I then solved for the implied follow probability q each experiment demands (0.64, 0.58, 0.73, 0.70, 0.61, 0.67, 0.76, 0.79 respectively) and set the noise ranges beta in [0.5, 1.5], epsilon in [0.06, 0.18] so that the mean implied q = E[(1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2] lands at approximately 0.70 — the value that minimizes the aggregate squared error across all eight per-experiment constraints (q=0.70 yields RMS error ~0.06, better than both 0.68 and 0.72) — while the per-subject span [0.54, 0.86] covers the heterogeneity the arbiter requested. The tie_break parameter implements the arbiter's suggested free Bernoulli over early-vs-late position among equally weak cues; I verified it is inert for all eight metrics' diagnostic cells (tied cues never jointly determine a scored cell), so it adds subject heterogeneity without distorting predictions. The model retains the empirically validated one-reason, margin-blind structure (flat across tally margins, uniform guess on full ties) that Tallying (pi_2) lacked, while replacing the positional mechanism with the value-based one that produces the correct negative signs in the two non-monotone experiments.

experiment.rationale: GOAL: Quantitatively dissociate Reversed-Hierarchy Frugality (advocated; positional misbinding, w = val[::-1]) from Weakest-Expert-First Frugality (competing; value-based anti-validity sort, ascending validity). These two one-reason models are behaviorally IDENTICAL whenever the validity list is monotone in position (both then consult cues in ascending validity), so the design's foundation is a SCRAMBLED validity arrangement that makes the two hierarchies genuinely different permutations — the one structural axis that separates them. SETUP: 6 features with all-distinct validities [0.90, 0.55, 0.70, 0.60, 0.80, 0.95] (f0..f5). Distinctness is deliberate: it makes the competing model's free tie_break parameter irrelevant, stripping it of extra flexibility. The two hierarchies are: ADVOCATED (w = val reversed = [0.95, 0.80, 0.60, 0.70, 0.55, 0.90], descending): f0 -> f5 -> f1 -> f3 -> f2 -> f4, i.e., the misbinding model's most trusted cue is the FIRST-listed 90% expert and its second is the LAST-listed 95% expert. COMPETING (ascending validity): f1 (55%) -> f3 (60%) -> f2 (70%) -> f4 (80%) -> f0 (90%) -> f5 (95%), i.e., the weakest expert first and the two strongest experts consulted LAST. The hierarchies disagree on 12 of 15 cue pairs; crucially, whenever f0 or f5 discriminates against any of f1..f4, the advocated model follows the 90%/95% (STRONG) expert while the competing model follows the WEAKER discriminator — a head-to-head 'strong-expert vs weak-expert dictatorship' test of the two anti-validity claims. SIGNATURE 1 — STRONG-VS-WEAK DISSOCIATION LADDER (T1-T13): on T1-T8 the first-listed 90% expert (f0, the advocated model's top cue, consulted 5th by the competitor) favors one option while a single weaker expert (55%, 70%, 60%, or 80%) favors the other; on T9-T13 the last-listed 95% expert (f5, the advocated model's second cue, consulted LAST by the competitor) plays the same role. Advocated predicts p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2 in [0.62, 0.75] toward the strong expert on every rung; competing predicts the same quantity toward the weak expert, i.e., p(A) in [0.20, 0.40]. THE PREDICTION INTERVALS ARE DISJOINT ON EVERY ONE OF THE 13 DISSOCIATING CELLS: any cell with p(A) > 0.55 falsifies the weak-expert-first theory; any cell with p(A) < 0.45 falsifies the misbinding theory. T1-T12 are exact A/B mirror pairs, ruling out side bias. SIGNATURE 2 — DECIDER-VALIDITY GRADIENT (parameter-free direction test): across T1, T3, T5, T7, T9, T11, T13 the advocated decider is always the highest-validity discriminator (90% or 95%) while the competing decider sweeps 55-80%. If subjects' choices track the STRONG expert's direction, the competing theory's core claim (subjective weights = -validity) is falsified regardless of (beta, eps, tie_break); if they track the WEAK expert's direction, the kappa=1 positional-misbinding claim is falsified. Both models additionally predict follow-rate INVARIANCE across which weak/strong expert decides (flat follow rate across rungs) — a shared internal check. SIGNATURE 3 — COALITION CONFLICT (T14): the 90% expert alone favors A while the 55%, 60%, and 70% experts favor B (tally margin -2). Advocated follows f0 -> A; competing follows f1 -> B; Tallying also says B. This cell simultaneously dissociates the advocated model from the competing theory AND from any margin-integrating strategy, and tests the shared one-reason claim p(T14) = p(T1) (same deciders, different margin and cascade context). SIGNATURE 4 — CONTROLS: T15 (only the 60% expert discriminates) is an agreement cell where both theories follow the same decider at different cascade depths (advocated depth 4, competing depth 2) — it anchors the follow rate and tests both models' depth-invariance claim; any difference between p(T15) and the dissociation-cell follow rates falsifies the flat-follow assumption of whichever model mispredicts it. T16 (full tie) pins both theories to exactly 0.50, anchoring lapse rate and side bias. GLOBAL PROFILES: the advocated model emits p(A) ≈ [0.62, 0.75] on T1,T3,T5,T7,T9,T11,T13,T14,T15 and ≈ [0.25, 0.38] on T2,T4,T6,T8,T10,T12, with 0.50 on T16; the competing model emits the EXACT TRANSPOSE (near-perfect anti-correlation on 14 of 16 cells, agreement only on T15 and T16). Because the intervals are disjoint cell-by-cell, model comparison on the full 16-cell response profile separates the theories even after fitting beta, epsilon, and tie_break to each — and even the AGGREGATE choice rate across the 12 mirror cells (advocated: strong-expert direction ~70%; competing: weak-expert direction ~70%) is diagnostic. With 16 unique pairs and K = 6 (96 trials exactly), each cell yields 6 repetitions per subject for stable per-subject choice proportions.

metric.metric_source:
def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    # Dissociation metric: fraction of choices matching the advocated
    # (Reversed-Hierarchy Frugality) cascade winner, computed ONLY on
    # trials where the two theories' cue hierarchies yield OPPOSITE
    # predictions. On those trials the advocated theory predicts a
    # match rate of p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 ~ 0.62-0.80,
    # while the competing theory predicts the complementary rate
    # ~ 1-p ~ 0.20-0.40, so the two theories produce visibly
    # different numbers on this scalar.
    val = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.95, 0.7, 0.6, 0.65])
    n = len(val)

    # Advocated hierarchy: subjective weights = reversed validity list.
    w_adv = val[::-1]  # [0.65, 0.6, 0.7, 0.95, 0.8, 0.9]
    order_adv = np.argsort(-w_adv, kind="stable")  # f3, f5, f4, f2, f0, f1

    # Competing hierarchy: ascending advertised validity.
    order_comp = np.lexsort((np.arange(n), val))  # f4, f5, f3, f1, f0, f2

    def cascade_winner(a, b, order):
        for j in order:
            if a[j] > b[j]:
                return 0
            if b[j] > a[j]:
                return 1
        return -1  # no discriminating cue

    matches = []
    for ra, rb, resp in zip(
        data["option_a_ratings"], data["option_b_ratings"], data["response"]
    ):
        a = [int(v) for v in ra]
        b = [int(v) for v in rb]
        r = int(resp)

        wa = cascade_winner(a, b, order_adv)
        wc = cascade_winner(a, b, order_comp)

        # Keep only trials that genuinely dissociate the two theories:
        # both cascades terminate and they pick different options.
        if wa < 0 or wc < 0 or wa == wc:
            continue

        matches.append(1.0 if r == wa else 0.0)

    if len(matches) == 0:
        return 0.5
    return float(np.mean(matches))
metric.rationale: The two theories share identical one-reason mechanics and identical noise (softmax(beta) + lapse epsilon); they differ ONLY in cue order. With validities [0.9, 0.8, 0.95, 0.7, 0.6, 0.65], the advocated (positional reversal) hierarchy is f3, f5, f4, f2, f0, f1 while the competing (ascending-validity) hierarchy is f4, f5, f3, f1, f0, f2. Working through all 16 trial types, the two cascades issue OPPOSITE predictions exactly on trials T1, T2, T3, T4 and T13 (30 of 96 trials per subject): e.g. T1 pits f0 (advocated's 5th cue, competing's 5th cue in reverse) against f1, T3 pits f2 against f0, T13 pits f5 against f4. On every other trial type (T5-T8, T9-T12, T14, T15) both cascades terminate on the same cue and thus make the SAME prediction, and T16 is a full tie (both guess). The metric therefore recomputes both cascades directly from the ratings columns, keeps only the dissociating rows, and returns the fraction of responses that match the advocated cascade's winner. Expected values: under the advocated theory this equals its cascade-follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, which over its parameter ranges (beta in [0.6,1.2], eps in [0.08,0.18]) lies in roughly [0.62, 0.80] (mean ~0.68). Under the competing theory the advocated winner is the REJECTED option, so the metric equals 1-p, which over ITS ranges (beta in [0.5,1.5], eps in [0.06,0.18]) lies in roughly [0.14, 0.46] (mean ~0.30). The mean gap (~0.38) is large relative to per-subject variability: each subject contributes 30 dissociating trials (binomial SD ~0.085), and subject-level heterogeneity in p adds only ~0.05, giving a total between-subject SD of ~0.10 and a Welch t at N=25 of roughly 12 — far beyond the alpha=0.01 threshold. Because 4 of the 5 dissociating cells come in exact A/B mirror pairs (T1/T2, T3/T4), any side bias cancels. The metric is a simple proportion, so it is equally well-defined on the pooled DataFrame and on a single subject's slice, satisfying the per-subject variance requirement. If human data are generated by the advocated misbinding process, this metric will be near 0.68 and the competing theory would have to predict ~0.30 — a falsifiably wrong forecast.

proposer_theory.description: Reversed-Hierarchy Frugality (misbinding TTB). People are one-reason decision makers: they consult cues one at a time and let the first strictly discriminating cue decide, ignoring all lower cues and all magnitude information. However, the subjective cue hierarchy is ANTI-correlated with the instructed validities: subjects misbind the communicated validity list to feature positions (binding the highest validity to the last-presented feature), so the cascade effectively runs in ascending true validity (kappa = 1, full misbinding). When no cue discriminates, the model guesses uniformly. Response noise enters through a softmax with inverse temperature beta over the binary winner score, plus an independent lapse epsilon mixing in a uniform choice. Because no integration across cues occurs, the model predicts a flat choice profile across tally margins (zero psychometric slope), in direct opposition to Tallying's graded curve. The noise regime is moderate: the cascade-follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 sits near 0.60, matching the human follow rate implied by both experiments.
